"My aunt will be down presently, Mr. Nuttel," said the niece, a very self-possessed young lady of fifteen. "In the meantime you must put up with me."

Framton Nuttel murmured something he hoped was gracious toward the niece without slighting the aunt who was still to come. He was supposed to be undergoing a nerve cure, and he privately doubted that a series of formal calls on total strangers was likely to do his nerves any good.

His sister had seen it differently. "I know exactly what will happen," she had told him while he packed for his rural retreat. "You'll bury yourself down there and speak to no one, and all that moping will leave your nerves worse than ever." So she had written him letters of introduction to everyone she knew in the district. "Some of them were quite nice," she had added, "as far as I can remember." He had brought one of those letters with him that afternoon, and it was to present it to Mrs. Sappleton that he now sat waiting in her drawing room.

"Do you know many of the people round here?" asked the niece, once the silence had gone on long enough.

"Hardly a soul," said Framton. "My sister stayed at the rectory here about four years ago." He said it with real regret, for he was beginning to wish she had never thought of the letters at all.

"Then you know practically nothing about my aunt?"

"Only her name and address," he admitted. As he spoke he glanced about the room and wondered whether Mrs. Sappleton was married or widowed. Something about the place, a pipe-rack perhaps, or the heavy boots by the fender, suggested that a man lived there.

"Her great tragedy happened exactly three years ago," said the child. "That would be after your sister's time."

"Her tragedy?" Framton repeated. In this restful countryside, tragedies seemed somehow out of place.

"You may wonder why we keep that window wide open on an October afternoon," said the niece, nodding toward a large French window that opened onto a lawn.

"It is quite warm for the time of year," said Framton. "But surely that window has nothing to do with the tragedy?"

"Three years ago to the day, her husband and her two young brothers went out through that window for a day's shooting. They never came back. They were crossing the moor to their favourite snipe-shooting ground, and all three were engulfed in a treacherous bog. It had been a dreadfully wet summer, you see. Ground that was safe in other years gave way that year without the slightest warning. Their bodies were never recovered." Her voice lost its composure and grew faltering. "Their little brown spaniel was lost with them. My poor aunt believes they will come back someday, the three of them and the dog, and walk in through that window just as they always did. That's why it's kept open every evening until dusk. She often tells me how they went out, her husband with his white waterproof coat over his arm, and Ronnie, her youngest brother, singing 'Bertie, why do you bound?' to tease her, because she always said that song got on her nerves." The girl gave a small shudder. "Do you know, sometimes on still evenings like this I get a creepy feeling that they will all walk in through that window."

It was a relief to Framton when the aunt bustled into the room, apologizing for being so late.

"I hope Vera has been keeping you amused," she said.

"She has been very interesting," said Framton.

"I hope you don't mind the open window," said Mrs. Sappleton briskly. "My husband and brothers will be home from shooting soon, and they always come in that way. They've been after snipe in the marshes today, so they'll make a fine mess of my carpets."

She chattered on cheerfully about the shooting, the scarcity of birds, and the prospects for duck in the winter. To Framton it was all perfectly horrible. He tried to steer the conversation toward something less ghastly and succeeded only in part. He was aware that his hostess was giving him only a fragment of her attention, and that her eyes kept straying past him to the open window and the lawn beyond. It was certainly an unfortunate coincidence, he thought, that he should have called on the very anniversary of the tragedy.

"The doctors all agree in ordering me complete rest," he announced, "and an absence of mental excitement, and no violent physical exercise of any kind. On the question of diet, however, they disagree entirely."

Framton laboured under the delusion, common among a great many people, that strangers and chance acquaintances are hungry for every last detail of one's ailments, their causes, and their cure. He went on at some length.

"No?" said Mrs. Sappleton, in a voice that only narrowly escaped a yawn. Then all at once she brightened into alert attention, though not at anything Framton had said.

"Here they are at last!" she cried. "Just in time for tea. And don't they look muddy, up to the eyes!"

Framton turned toward the niece with a look meant to convey sympathetic understanding. But the child was staring out through the open window, her eyes filled with dazed horror. A chill of nameless fear crept over Framton, and slowly he turned in his seat to look out of the window.
